Looking slightly to one side of a faint object, so its light falls on the more sensitive edge of your eye.
The circle of sky your binoculars show at once. Its width in degrees is printed on most binoculars.
The crowded, rounded swarm of stars at the center of a spiral galaxy.
A cool giant whose atmosphere is rich in carbon, which filters out blue light and makes it look deep red.
A pulsing supergiant that brightens and fades on a strict rhythm. The slower the rhythm, the more light it really gives off.
The other star in a pair, usually the fainter one.
One of 88 official regions of the sky, each named after the old star figure inside it, such as Orion or Cygnus.
Two stars that look close together. Some orbit each other; others only line up by chance.
When a giant's churning layers carry freshly made elements, such as carbon, up from its core to its surface.
A dark band of dust cutting across a galaxy or the Milky Way, blocking the light from behind.
Atoms crushed together in a star's core into heavier ones, releasing the energy that makes the star shine.
The flat, spinning pancake of stars, gas and dust where the Sun and most young stars of our galaxy live.
The huge, thin sphere of old stars and globular clusters surrounding a galaxy's flat disk.
A dense ball of hundreds of thousands of very old stars, orbiting our galaxy far from its flat disk.
The second-lightest element. Stars make it by fusing hydrogen, and heavier stars later fuse it into carbon and oxygen.
The lightest and most common element, the main fuel stars burn for most of their lives.
Light with longer waves than red, invisible to the eye. It passes through dust and shows cool things.
Several telescopes linked to act as one giant one, sharp enough to measure star sizes or split very close pairs.
The distance light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion km. It measures distance, not time.
The total light a star really gives off, however near or far it is. The Sun's is the usual yardstick.
A huge, unstable blue star that brightens and erupts unpredictably, throwing off shells of gas.
The astronomer's brightness scale. Smaller numbers are brighter; each step of 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness.
The long, steady adult stage of a star's life, when it quietly fuses hydrogen in its core, as the Sun does now.
Our home galaxy, and the faint band of light it makes across the sky because we see its disk from inside.
A cloud of gas and dust in space. Some glow, some reflect starlight and some block the light behind them.
A loose, spread-out family of young, hot, heavy stars that formed together and are drifting apart.
A loose family of stars born together from one cloud, usually a few hundred million years old or younger.
The tiny shift of a nearby star against far ones as Earth circles the Sun. The smaller the shift, the farther the star.
A star still forming: a collapsing ball of gas that is not yet hot enough in its core to fuse hydrogen.
A star that swells and shrinks in a rhythm, getting brighter and fainter as it does.
An ageing star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to many times its old size, cooling to orange or red.
The mass of the Sun, used as the unit for weighing stars.

A galaxy shaped like a flat disk with curving arms of young stars and gas around a central bulge.
A heavy star late in life, swollen to enormous size and pouring out thousands of times the Sun's light.
The explosion of a star, briefly outshining a whole galaxy of ordinary stars. Heavy stars end this way.
Light with shorter waves than violet, invisible to the eye. Hot stars pour out lots of it.
A star whose brightness changes, because it pulses, erupts, or is eclipsed by a partner.
The leftover core of a Sun-like star: about Earth's size but as heavy as the Sun, slowly cooling for billions of years.

journeys.title: Orion's Record Book
journeys.drivingQuestion: What are the most extreme things you can see tonight, and how do we know?
journeys.hook: To crown the biggest star you first need its distance, its color and its power.
journeys.story: Begin with the Hyades and follow the records upward until Betelgeuse, where the question is no longer how bright or how hot but how big. Nobody has ever laid a ruler across a star, so the answer has to be built from every number gathered along the way.
journeys.payoff: From the Hyades to Betelgeuse, every record rested on the measurements below it, and the last of them, the size of a star, needed all of them at once. A star's width comes from how much light it pours out and how hot each patch of its surface glows, and those two numbers in turn need its distance and its color. Size records tell stories of their own, too: the largest stars are heavy stars swollen near the ends of their lives, the smallest are the crushed cores of dead ones, and the fastest spinners are squashed out of round.

stops.name: Hyades

getThere.text: Find the Hyades by eye, the V of stars around orange Aldebaran in Taurus, about 60° up in the south-east. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: A cluster is a family whose members share one distance, so the nearest family of all is where stars of many kinds can be compared side by side at a known range.

card.question: How can a cluster’s colors tell its age?
card.glance: A big V of stars spilling past the edges of the field, several of them yellow-orange.
card.see: The V of the Bull’s face in Taurus is too big for one view, so sweep along each arm. A few cluster stars are tinted orange among the white ones. Aldebaran, the brightest orange point at one tip, is the odd one out.
card.understand: Because the Hyades are so close, the Hipparcos satellite could measure the parallax of individual members and map the cluster in three dimensions, with its core about 150 light-years away. The family is about 625 million years old, five times older than the Pleiades. In that time its heaviest blue stars have died, and the next heaviest have swollen into orange giants.
card.answer: The color of the brightest members is the clock: blue-white stars mean the heavy ones are still alive, while orange giants among white and yellow stars mean that era has passed.
card.wonder: Gaia has traced stars escaping from it into two long tails, one leading and one trailing the cluster along its orbit, each stretching for hundreds of light-years.
card.connect: The brightest star in the V, Aldebaran, does not belong to the family at all.

lens.question: How far away is the nearest star cluster, and why does that matter?
lens.why: A cluster is a family whose members share one distance, so the nearest family of all is where stars of many kinds can be compared side by side at a known range.
lens.look: The V of the Bull's face in Taurus is too big for one view, so sweep along each arm. Every family member you pass sits at nearly the same distance, which makes their differences in brightness and color real; Aldebaran, the bright orange star at one tip, lies in front and does not count.
lens.answer: The core of the Hyades lies about 150 light-years away, closer than any other true cluster, so its stars spill past the edges of your field. Because every member shares that distance, the family works like a set of labeled samples: compare a far cluster's stars with these and you can tell how much farther it is.
lens.story: Long before satellites, the Hyades gave up their distance through perspective. The members move through space in parallel, so their paths across the sky seem to converge on one point, the way railway tracks meet at the horizon, and the angle to that point, combined with each star's speed toward us read from its spectrum, turns a drift in arcseconds into a speed in kilometers per second. Set the two side by side and the distance falls out, and for most of the twentieth century this was the rung on which brighter, farther yardsticks were calibrated.

stops.name: W Orionis

getThere.text: From the Hyades, slide down about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°) to W Orionis, in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Betelgeuse is famous for its cool red glow, yet a much fainter star near Bellatrix runs cooler still.
stops.transitionText: With a distance settled at the Hyades, the records move to heat, and W Orionis is where the thermometer is read.

card.question: Why does W Orionis glow so warmly red?
card.glance: An orange-red star in western Orion, easy in binoculars.
card.see: Look about 7° south-west of Bellatrix, Orion’s western shoulder. Among white field stars it stands out as orange-red, and a slight defocus boosts the color.
card.understand: W Orionis is an old giant that fuses helium into carbon in a shell deep inside, and every so often its churning outer layers reach down and dredge some of that carbon up to the surface. In its cool atmosphere, about 2,700 K, the carbon forms molecules that soak up blue light. It also varies slowly in brightness, over about seven months.
card.answer: Carbon molecules in its cool atmosphere filter out the blue and leave a warm red glow, like a lamp seen through smoked glass.
card.wonder: Stars like this are a major source of the carbon in the galaxy, including the carbon in you.
card.connect: An even redder carbon star waits in Lepus, below Orion.

lens.question: Which star in Orion runs even cooler than Betelgeuse?
lens.why: Betelgeuse is famous for its cool red glow, yet a much fainter star near Bellatrix runs cooler still.
lens.look: About 7° south-west of Bellatrix, Orion's western shoulder, look for an orange-red star among white field stars; a slight defocus boosts the color. Then glance at Betelgeuse: the famous red star looks paler orange beside this one, though it is far brighter.
lens.answer: W Orionis is roughly 900 degrees cooler than Betelgeuse at the surface, and the carbon in its atmosphere reddens it further. It looks faint because it lies about three times farther away and gives out far less light, so the cold record and the brightness record go to different stars.
lens.story: Betelgeuse and W Orionis are cool in different chemistries. In Betelgeuse oxygen outnumbers carbon, so its spectrum is striped with bands of titanium oxide; in W Orionis carbon has won, and bands of carbon molecules take their place. Each set of bands deepens in a known way as the gas cools, which is how two red stars of different makeup can still be put on one thermometer.

stops.name: Rigel

getThere.text: Move down and to the right about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (10°), and Rigel is there, still in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Brightness alone crowned Sirius, and Rigel, Orion's blue-white foot, is the place to see what brightness hides, because its light has a far longer road to travel.
stops.transitionText: Temperature, as W Orionis showed, is only half of a star's story; for Rigel the questions become how much light it pours out and how much matter it holds.

card.question: How does Rigel, a hundred times farther than Sirius, manage to look almost as bright?
card.glance: A brilliant blue-white star at Orion’s foot, diagonally across from orange Betelgeuse.
card.see: Rigel is Orion’s foot, the brilliant blue-white star diagonally across from Betelgeuse. Hold it in the field and its icy color is unmistakable, especially just after a look at the orange shoulder. A faint companion sits very close, but binoculars lose it in the glare.
card.understand: Its color says the surface is about 12,000 K, twice as hot as the Sun’s, glowing the way metal does when heated past red and yellow. Its distance comes from parallax: as Earth circles the Sun, Rigel shifts against far more distant stars by a few thousandths of an arcsecond, and the Hipparcos satellite caught that tiny wobble well enough to put it about 860 light-years away. Light fades with the square of distance, so anything this bright from that far must be extraordinary.
card.answer: Rigel pours out tens of thousands of times the Sun’s light, which is how it rivals nearby Sirius from a hundred times farther away.
card.wonder: The light reaching you tonight left Rigel in the 12th century, while stone castles were rising across medieval Europe.
card.connect: Brightness fooled you here, and not far away a dazzling star owes its glare mostly to living next door.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photo of the binocular field around Rigel, 4° wide; Rigel is the star at the centre, between the four marks. North up, east left. A long photographic exposure, so it shows more stars and colour than binoculars do.

lens.question: How much light must Rigel pour out to rival Sirius from a hundred times farther?
lens.why: Brightness alone crowned Sirius, and Rigel, Orion's blue-white foot, is the place to see what brightness hides, because its light has a far longer road to travel.
lens.look: Rigel is Orion's brilliant blue-white foot, diagonally across from Betelgeuse. Sirius, low to the south-east, outshines it only a few times over, even though Rigel lies about a hundred times farther away.
lens.answer: Rigel pours out about 83,000 times the Sun's light, thousands of times what Sirius manages, and nothing less would let it come so close to Sirius in our sky across a hundred times the distance. A furnace that strong burns through its fuel quickly, which is why the most powerful stars are always young ones, and why Rigel will not last nearly as long as the Sun.
lens.story: The arithmetic behind that number is the inverse-square law: light spreading from a star thins out over the surface of an ever larger sphere, so at three times the distance each square meter of your eye receives nine times less. Run the law backward with Rigel's measured faintness and distance and out comes its output, after one more correction for the ultraviolet the eye misses. The step is simple, but every power record on this ladder is built from it.

stops.name: θ¹ Orionis C

getThere.text: Move left about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°), and θ¹ Orionis C is there, still in Orion.

stops.whyHere: A nebula's glow is a meter for the power of the stars inside it, and in Orion that meter points to one bright knot in the core.
stops.transitionText: Like Rigel, θ¹ Orionis C reveals its true output only once its distance is known, and side by side the two show how little a star's looks say about its power.

card.question: What makes the Orion Nebula glow?
card.glance: One bright point inside the glowing heart of the Orion Nebula, in Orion’s Sword.
card.see: Center the Orion Nebula, the fuzzy middle star of the Sword below the Belt, and look at the bright knot in its core. Binoculars merge the four Trapezium stars into one point, and θ¹ Orionis C is the brightest of them.
card.understand: θ¹ Orionis C is a young pair of very heavy stars, together about 44 times the Sun’s mass. That weight comes from watching the two swing through their closest approach with an infrared interferometer and applying the same orbital laws that weigh the planets. Stars this heavy are fiercely hot, and they flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light energetic enough to tear electrons off hydrogen atoms.
card.answer: When the electrons fall back, the hydrogen glows in its own particular colors like a neon sign, and this one system supplies most of the ultraviolet that keeps the sign lit; switch it off and most of the nebula would go dark.
card.wonder: It is only about a million years old: when it began to shine, our ancestors were already walking upright.
card.connect: Not every star born here stays home, and one of the Trapezium’s siblings was flung all the way into Auriga.

lens.beat: Power plant of the Orion Nebula
lens.question: Which single star system lights most of the Orion Nebula?
lens.why: A nebula's glow is a meter for the power of the stars inside it, and in Orion that meter points to one bright knot in the core.
lens.answer: θ¹ Orionis C does, a heavyweight pair at the heart of the nebula that supplies most of the ultraviolet keeping the cloud alight. Its mass, rather than its distance or its looks, is what makes it the power plant, because the heavier a star, the more steeply its output climbs.
lens.story: Every hydrogen atom the star strips must sooner or later recapture an electron and glow, so the nebula's total hydrogen light, or its radio glow, counts how many atom-stripping photons the star pours out each second. That count is a measure of power in the ultraviolet, where the eye sees nothing, and for the Orion Nebula it points to one star of the hottest kind. Astronomers use the same bookkeeping on nebulae in other galaxies to weigh up stars they cannot see one by one.

stops.name: Betelgeuse

getThere.text: From θ¹ Orionis C, slide up and to the left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°) to Betelgeuse, still in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Orion's red shoulder is the size record most people know, and it is worth asking whether fame and size go together.
stops.transitionText: A star's power and its temperature together decide its size, so after θ¹ Orionis C the records turn to bodies, and Betelgeuse holds one of them.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine almost everything around it?
card.glance: A bright orange-red star on Orion’s shoulder, whose color blooms when you nudge the focus slightly off.
card.see: Betelgeuse marks Orion’s eastern shoulder, the bright orange star opposite blue-white Rigel. Turn the focus a little past sharp and the point blooms into a small disk whose orange-red suddenly becomes obvious; swing to Rigel to feel the contrast. Its brightness drifts over months, so judge it fresh each time.
card.understand: A star’s color is a thermometer, and Betelgeuse’s says its surface is only about 3,600 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so each square meter of it shines more feebly than the Sun’s. The surprise is how many square meters there are. Astronomers timed its slow pulsations and fed them into models of how heavy stars age, and out came about 18 Suns’ worth of matter swollen to some 760 times the Sun’s width.
card.answer: That is the whole trick: a dim glow spread over an almost absurd amount of surface still adds up to far more light than the Sun will ever give.
card.wonder: Put Betelgeuse where the Sun is and its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars.
card.connect: Heavy stars like this do not fade quietly, and the wreckage of one that already exploded lies next door in Taurus.

image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: VLT/SPHERE images of Betelgeuse’s surface before (January 2019) and during the Great Dimming (December 2019 – March 2020).

lens.beat: One of the largest naked-eye stars
lens.question: Is Betelgeuse the largest star you can see, or only the most famous?
lens.why: Orion's red shoulder is the size record most people know, and it is worth asking whether fame and size go together.
lens.answer: It is one of the largest the naked eye can reach, but not the champion: VY Canis Majoris, a binocular star in the Great Dog, is nearly twice as wide, and the Garnet Star may also be bigger. Betelgeuse earns its fame by being close, about 550 light-years away, so its disk spans some 43 thousandths of an arcsecond, wide enough for big telescopes to map.
lens.story: Betelgeuse was the first star beyond the Sun whose width was ever measured. In 1920 Albert Michelson and Francis Pease mounted a steel beam across the top of the great Mount Wilson telescope, with mirrors that could be slid apart along it, and watched the interference pattern vanish when the mirrors stood about three meters apart, the separation that matched the star's disk. Every size record since descends from that experiment.

journeys.drivingQuestion: How do astronomers measure distances that no one could ever travel?
journeys.hook: Every distance in the sky rests on the one below it, and the first on Earth's orbit.
journeys.story: From Capella to the Andromeda Galaxy, tonight's stops climb a ladder of rulers right out of the Milky Way. Each rung is calibrated on the one beneath, so the distance of another galaxy is tied, step by step, to the yearly wobble of the nearest stars.
journeys.payoff: The Andromeda Galaxy lies outside the Milky Way altogether, yet its distance is tied to every rung beneath it. Those rungs are the yearly shift of nearby stars, the families that turned those shifts into true brightness, and the pulsing stars calibrated on both. Find a pulsing star in another galaxy, time its beat, and how faint it looks tells you how far it is. That one trick, resting on Earth's orbit, turned the faint smudges of the sky into other galaxies and gave the universe a measurable size.

stops.name: Capella

getThere.text: Find Capella by eye, the bright yellow star of Auriga, about 65° up in the north-east. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Capella opens the ladder with a distance measured as directly as anything in astronomy, by the shift that Earth's own orbit produces.

card.question: How can two giant stars hide inside a single point of light?
card.glance: The golden leader of Auriga, riding high on winter evenings.
card.see: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings, leading the pentagon of Auriga. Its creamy, slightly golden tint sits halfway between Rigel’s ice and Aldebaran’s orange. Just south of it lies the thin triangle of fainter stars called the Kids.
card.understand: The two stars circle each other every 104 days, so close that only interferometers, which combine several telescopes into one sharp eye, can separate them. Follow the orbit and the same laws that weigh the planets give the masses: about two and a half Suns each. Add each star’s measured size and temperature and something odd appears, because one already burns helium in its core, the fuel of a star’s later years, while its near-twin is only now swelling into a giant.
card.answer: Each giant is about ten times wider than the Sun, yet from 43 light-years their whole orbit shrinks to a speck that only an interferometer can open up.
card.wonder: A difference of a few percent in mass was enough to put two stars born together in different chapters of life.
card.connect: Next door in the Kids, a stranger pair hides one star inside a vast dark disk.

lens.question: How far is Capella, and why can that number be trusted?
lens.why: Capella opens the ladder with a distance measured as directly as anything in astronomy, by the shift that Earth's own orbit produces.
lens.look: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star leading Auriga, high overhead on winter evenings. It outshines everything around it, and brightness like that is a hint of closeness, but not yet a measurement.
lens.answer: Hipparcos measured a yearly shift of about 76 thousandths of an arcsecond, which puts Capella about 43 light-years away, and the only assumption behind that number is the size of Earth's orbit. Stars measured this cleanly become reference points for how bright each kind of star truly is, the knowledge the next rungs depend on.
lens.story: Capella offers a rare second route to its distance. Its two stars have been tracked both in angle, by interferometers, and in speed, from the Doppler shift of their light; the speeds give the orbit's true size in kilometers and the interferometers its size in arcseconds, and the ratio of the two is the distance. That orbital parallax agrees with the satellite's yearly shift, two independent rulers meeting on one star.

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (20°) to the Alpha Persei Cluster, in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: The Alpha Persei Cluster spreads around Mirfak, a family near enough that Gaia can measure nearly every bright member.
stops.transitionText: Capella was measured on its own, by geometry, but one star teaches you about one star; at the Alpha Persei Cluster the same geometry, applied to a whole family, becomes a rule that holds for every star of a kind.

card.question: What does a star family look like from up close?
card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains. It is too big for most telescopes to frame, so binoculars or the eye alone take it in whole.
card.understand: This is an open cluster, a family of stars born together from one cloud, and Gaia picks out its members by their shared motion, like spotting a family walking together through a crowd. Its age comes from a subtle clue: the lightest members slowly destroy the lithium inside them, so the line between stars that still have lithium and those that have lost it works like a clock. Here it reads about 90 million years.
card.answer: Like the Alpha Persei Cluster: at 566 light-years its members spread over several Moon widths, a spray only binoculars can frame. Farther away, the same family would shrink into a small knot.
card.wonder: This family was born while dinosaurs still had tens of millions of years left.
card.connect: The Double Cluster, more than ten times farther away, shows how small a star family looks from across the galaxy.

lens.question: How does Gaia turn a scattered family around Mirfak into one precise distance?
lens.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster spreads around Mirfak, a family near enough that Gaia can measure nearly every bright member.
lens.look: Center Mirfak and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too big for most telescopes to frame. Mirfak itself fits the family's pattern, a bright member rather than a stranger in front.
lens.answer: Each member's parallax is small and a little uncertain, but averaging nearly a thousand of them shrinks the uncertainty enormously, and the cluster comes out about 566 light-years away. With that distance fixed, the true brightness of every kind of star in it is known, ready to be laid against clusters too far for parallax.
lens.story: The family stands out in Gaia's data as a tight knot in motion: plot every star's drift across the sky and the cluster's members pile into one spot while the field stars scatter. Only after that sorting are the parallaxes combined, and Mirfak, measured on its own, comes out at the family's distance, which is how we know it belongs.

stops.name: Stock 2

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°) to Stock 2, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Stock 2 is a big, loose family beside the Double Cluster, close enough that binoculars show many of the very stars the comparison uses.
stops.transitionText: Lay the stars of Stock 2 against the patterns set by families like the Alpha Persei Cluster, and the gap in brightness becomes a distance, the first rung measured by comparison rather than by geometry.

card.question: Are two clusters side by side in the sky really neighbors?
card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars in Cassiopeia, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north, and a large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the “Muscleman”. Use the widest field you have, because a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Gaia measures each member’s parallax and averages them, which pins down a cluster’s distance far better than any single star could. For Stock 2 it gives about 1,200 light-years, and for the Double Cluster over 7,000. The ages differ too: Stock 2 has lost its hottest blue stars, a sign of a few hundred million years, while the Double Cluster’s still blaze.
card.answer: These two are not: Stock 2 is about six times nearer and far older than the glittering pair beside it, proof that clusters touching on the sky can live in completely different parts of the galaxy.
card.wonder: Gaia found about 3,000 members here, a big family hiding in plain sight because it is so spread out.
card.connect: Swing back to the Double Cluster: the nearer family looks bigger and looser, the farther one smaller and denser.

lens.question: Before Gaia, how could anyone measure a cluster too far for a clean parallax?
lens.why: Stock 2 is a big, loose family beside the Double Cluster, close enough that binoculars show many of the very stars the comparison uses.
lens.look: Stock 2 fills much of the field two degrees north of the Double Cluster, a loose spray in which some observers trace a little muscleman. Its stars look modest, yet many of them are hotter and more powerful than the Sun, dimmed only by distance.
lens.answer: Plot its steady adult stars by color and brightness, the band astronomers call the main sequence, and slide that band until it lines up with the same band in a cluster of known distance; the amount of sliding is the distance. The method works at any depth where the stars can still be seen, which is how the ladder outruns parallax. Gaia's parallaxes have since checked the slide, and it holds.
lens.story: This family is a hard case for the method because of its sprawl: its members cover more sky than several full Moons, mixed with thousands of unrelated stars in front and behind, which blur any plot of its colors and brightnesses. Before Gaia sorted members by their motions, any fit here had to guess at membership, and Gaia's census is what turned a loose sprinkle into a measured family.

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (7°) to the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), still in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: The Owl Cluster is far enough that its distance rests on its many members together, and that shared distance may also belong to the bright star at its eye.
stops.transitionText: Clusters like Stock 2 reach only as far as their ordinary stars can be seen, so the ladder needs rarer, more powerful stars whose true output can be pinned down, and the Owl Cluster belongs to that rung.

card.question: Does the Owl Cluster’s bright eye really belong to the cluster?
card.glance: Two bright “eyes” at one end of a small, elongated swarm in Cassiopeia, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other; the bright one is φ Cassiopeiae. A faint, slightly elongated spray trails away from them, and steady binoculars turn it into outstretched wings or arms.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,100 light-years away and only about 23 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life; if it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia’s parallax for φ Cas matches the cluster’s, but very bright stars are hard for Gaia to measure, and its speed toward us differs somewhat from older values.
card.answer: Probably, since the evidence leans toward membership, which would make the owl’s eye one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. The case is not closed, and that is part of the fun.
card.wonder: If φ Cas is a member, its light set out about 9,100 years ago, when one of the first towns, Çatalhöyük in Anatolia, was taking shape.
card.connect: M103, a degree from Ruchbah, is a cluster whose stars clearly belong together.

lens.beat: A cluster lends a star its distance
lens.question: How can a single bright star borrow its distance from the cluster around it?
lens.why: The Owl Cluster is far enough that its distance rests on its many members together, and that shared distance may also belong to the bright star at its eye.
lens.look: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, a bright star and a fainter one form the owl's eyes, with a faint elongated spray trailing away as wings. The bright eye is φ Cassiopeiae, the star whose membership is in question.
lens.answer: The cluster's hundreds of members, compared with nearby templates and measured by Gaia, put it about 9,100 light-years away, and a star that truly belongs shares that depth. If φ Cas does, its modest look hides enormous power, and borrowing a distance from a cluster is exactly how rare, powerful stars like the Cepheids had their true output pinned down.
lens.story: Borrowing works only if membership is real, and the test is the usual pair: the star must share the cluster's distance and its motion through space. For φ Cassiopeiae the distance fits while its speed toward us is a little off the cluster's, so astronomers still hedge, and every Cepheid in a cluster had to pass the same scrutiny before it could calibrate anything.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Sweep left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (18°) to the Andromeda Galaxy, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: The Andromeda Galaxy is where the pulsing-star ruler first left the Milky Way, and its history shows how every rung depends on the ones below.
stops.transitionText: From the Owl Cluster the ladder takes its longest step, because the brightest stars of known power can be picked out one by one in the Andromeda Galaxy, far beyond the Milky Way.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

lens.question: Why did Hubble's first distance to Andromeda come out less than half the true value?
lens.why: The Andromeda Galaxy is where the pulsing-star ruler first left the Milky Way, and its history shows how every rung depends on the ones below.
lens.look: From Mirach climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears: an obvious oval core and, with averted vision, a haze stretching about three degrees. M32 is a fuzzy star just south of the core.
lens.answer: The calibration of the Cepheid rule available to Hubble at the time was off, so every distance it gave came out too small, and fixing the lower rungs later stretched Andromeda out to about 2.5 million light-years. The ladder you climbed tonight is the corrected one, and at its top stands a galaxy whose light left before our species existed.
lens.story: Hubble's method was sound: he found pulsing stars in photographs of Andromeda, timed their beats, read off their true power from Leavitt's rule and compared it with how faint they looked. The weak point was the rule's zero point, borrowed from pulsing stars in our own galaxy that, as Walter Baade showed in 1952, were an older and fainter kind than Andromeda's Cepheids.

journeys.title: Cygnus, from Nursery to Embers
journeys.drivingQuestion: What happens to a star between its birth and its death?
journeys.hook: No one lives long enough to watch a star grow up, yet the sky shows every age at once.
journeys.story: Every star you will see tonight is at a different moment of the same life, and the stops run in the order a star lives them, right through to its death. Weight is the thread: the heavier a star, the faster it travels that road and the more violently it ends.
journeys.payoff: The sky holds every stage of a star's life at once, and tonight you read them in order, ending at the Dumbbell Nebula, what a star leaves behind. Clouds collapse into stars, families age from the top down, and old age swells each star until its fuel is gone. Then a star like the Sun lets its layers drift off around a cooling core, while a heavyweight collapses and explodes. Either way its gas returns to space richer than it began, and from such recycled gas the Sun, the Earth and we ourselves were made.

stops.name: IC 1396 and Trumpler 37
stops.plainClass: glowing gas cloud where stars form

getThere.text: Find Alderamin by eye, the brightest star of Cepheus, about 65° up in the north. From there, hop up about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°) to IC 1396 and Trumpler 37.

stops.whyHere: Every star begins in a cloud, and in IC 1396 a young cluster and the cold gas around it share one field, the raw material and the first results side by side.

card.question: Can one generation of stars trigger the birth of the next?
card.glance: A loose cluster around a star at the naked-eye limit, south of the Garnet Star in Cepheus, inside a huge faint nebula.
card.see: Put the deep-orange Garnet Star at the north edge of the field; about 1.5° south-south-west a scatter of stars gathers around a brighter one, HD 206267. Under a dark sky a faint glow may surround it, but expect stars rather than the pink cloud of photographs.
card.understand: The central star is really a group of very hot, heavy stars whose ultraviolet light makes the surrounding hydrogen glow. Where their light and winds squeeze the edges of the cloud, the gas is pressed dense enough for gravity to take over and collapse it into new stars. Infrared telescopes, which see through dust, found protostars less than a million years old inside the dark “Elephant’s Trunk” at the nebula’s edge, younger than the stars squeezing them.
card.answer: It can, and in IC 1396 the light and winds of hot young stars are pressing the edges of their cloud into new stars right now. Different corners of the cluster have different ages, a record of star birth spreading in waves.
card.wonder: In a few million years the heaviest stars here will swell into red supergiants like the Garnet Star at the edge of your field.
card.connect: NGC 7160, just to the north, shows the same family’s older generation, its birth cloud already gone.

lens.beat: Nursery: one generation sparks the next
lens.question: How much of the cloud at IC 1396's edge is actually turning into stars?
lens.why: Every star begins in a cloud, and in IC 1396 a young cluster and the cold gas around it share one field, the raw material and the first results side by side.
lens.look: Start at the Garnet Star and move about a degree and a half south-south-west to the scatter of stars around HD 206267. That bright central star is the group of hot stars doing the work; the glowing gas they press on is faint at best in binoculars.
lens.answer: So far only about five percent of the mass of the dark globule called the Elephant's Trunk has turned into protostars. Much of the rest will be boiled away by the hot stars' light before it can collapse, which is why clouds make stars so wastefully, and why their families soon find themselves standing in the open.
lens.story: The hot stars at the center are pushing a front of compressed gas into the cloud around them, and new stars form where that front arrives. Inside the Elephant's Trunk the young stars grow younger the deeper they lie in the globule, the pattern expected if the squeeze is moving inward and setting off collapse as it goes.

resolved.look: Start at the Garnet Star and move about a degree and a half south-south-west to the scatter of stars around HD 206267. That bright central star is the group of hot stars doing the work; the glowing gas they press on is faint at best in binoculars.
resolved.story: The hot stars at the center are pushing a front of compressed gas into the cloud around them, and new stars form where that front arrives. Inside the Elephant's Trunk the young stars grow younger the deeper they lie in the globule, the pattern expected if the squeeze is moving inward and setting off collapse as it goes.
resolved.understand: The central star is really a group of very hot, heavy stars whose ultraviolet light makes the surrounding hydrogen glow. Where their light and winds squeeze the edges of the cloud, the gas is pressed dense enough for gravity to take over and collapse it into new stars. Infrared telescopes, which see through dust, found protostars less than a million years old inside the dark “Elephant’s Trunk” at the nebula’s edge, younger than the stars squeezing them.
resolved.answer: So far only about five percent of the mass of the dark globule called the Elephant's Trunk has turned into protostars. Much of the rest will be boiled away by the hot stars' light before it can collapse, which is why clouds make stars so wastefully, and why their families soon find themselves standing in the open.
resolved.wonder: In a few million years the heaviest stars here will swell into red supergiants like the Garnet Star at the edge of your field.

stops.name: M39

getThere.text: Move up and to the left about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (9°), and M39 is there, in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: M39 is a family close enough for you to count its brightest members one by one.
stops.transitionText: The stars born in clouds like IC 1396 and Trumpler 37 will one day travel together as a family like M39, long after their birth gas has vanished.

card.question: How many stars of a nearby family can you count one by one?
card.glance: A large, bright, loose triangle of a few dozen stars north-east of Deneb, easy in any binoculars.
card.see: From Deneb, sweep about 9° east-north-east in Cygnus to a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon, standing out from the Milky Way. At your lowest power count the members, and notice that the brightest are all white or blue-white.
card.understand: Gaia shows these stars sharing one distance, about 965 light-years, and one motion through space: an open cluster, a family born together. A 2024 study of their spectra fits an age of roughly 430 million years, though another method gives a third of that, a reminder that cluster ages depend on models. The bluest heavyweights have burned out, and the brightest survivors are white stars of about three solar masses.
card.answer: You can count a few dozen, M39's brightest white stars standing out one by one, the visible tip of a family Gaia counts at over five hundred.
card.wonder: Aristotle may have noted it as a comet-like smudge around 325 BC, which would make it one of the first star clusters ever written down.
card.connect: NGC 6819, deeper in Cygnus, is several times older and has somehow held together.

lens.beat: A family in its middle years
lens.question: What happens to M39's family as its stars age?
lens.why: M39 is a family close enough for you to count its brightest members one by one.
lens.answer: It ages from the top down. Its brightest white stars are the next in line to spend their core hydrogen and swell into giants, and as each one does, the family's light grows a little fainter and warmer, just as it did when its bluest members burned out long ago.

stops.name: Deneb

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (9°) to Deneb, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Deneb is a heavyweight whose old age is happening fast.
stops.transitionText: In a family like M39 the heaviest stars are the first to spend their core hydrogen, and Deneb is a star that has already done so, now into its old age.

card.question: Why does the most powerful star of the Summer Triangle look the faintest?
card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, the swan's tail in Cygnus, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan, and the top of the Northern Cross. Sweep slowly around it and the field fills with countless faint stars, because here you are looking along the Milky Way; then glance back at Vega, which is plainly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away. Deneb is too far for a precise parallax, so its distance is still argued over, but the best estimate puts it around 2,600 light-years, roughly a hundred times farther. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star a hundred times farther must pour out ten thousand times more light just to keep up.
card.answer: Deneb only looks modest because it is so far away. It is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen to about 200 times the Sun's width and shining with something like 200,000 Suns, and even from that distance it nearly keeps pace with its neighbor.
card.wonder: If the best estimate is right, the light entering your eye tonight set out when Rome was still a small kingdom.
card.connect: Stars like Deneb do not stay white: the Garnet Star in Cepheus shows the red supergiant stage that lies ahead.

lens.beat: Aging supergiant on its way to red
lens.question: What is Deneb turning into?
lens.why: Deneb is a heavyweight whose old age is happening fast.
lens.look: Deneb is the bright white star at the tail of the swan, the top of the Northern Cross. Its white is the color of a heavyweight only partway to red; sweep about 16° north-north-east into Cepheus to the Garnet Star, a deep orange-red supergiant at the stage Deneb is heading for.
lens.answer: Deneb is most likely turning into a red supergiant. Its surface already shows nitrogen dredged up from the core, a sign that it has burned through its core hydrogen, and the best models have it swelling toward the red supergiant stage on its way to a supernova. For now it is a white star about 200 times the Sun's width, midway through that crossing.
lens.story: A heavy star burns hydrogen through a cycle that uses carbon as a go-between and turns much of it into nitrogen, so nitrogen showing up at the surface means material from the core has been mixed outward. In Deneb that mixing is strong enough to measure, one of the main clues that the star has finished its core hydrogen rather than still being in its prime.

stops.name: P Cygni

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (8°) to P Cygni, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: P Cygni is a heavyweight so luminous that it is already coming apart at the seams.
stops.transitionText: Every giant like Deneb eventually reaches the last stretch of its life, and P Cygni is a star already there, how it finishes set by the weight it was born with.

card.question: What happens when a star is almost too heavy to hold itself together?
card.glance: A modest 5th-magnitude star about 2½° south-west of Sadr, the center of the Northern Cross in Cygnus.
card.see: From Sadr, at the center of the Northern Cross, slide about 2½° south-west toward Albireo. P Cygni is a plain white point against the Milky Way, easy in binoculars, and nothing in the view hints at its power.
card.understand: P Cygni is a luminous blue variable, one of the heaviest and most luminous kinds of star. In a star this bright the outflowing light itself pushes on the gas almost as hard as gravity pulls it back, so the outer layers are barely held. It leaks mass in a fierce wind and now and then lets go of much more at once; the 1600 eruption threw off a shell that is still expanding today.
card.answer: It starts to come apart: light nearly overpowers gravity, and the star sheds itself in a steady wind and sudden outbursts like the one of 1600. Its name lives on in the P Cygni profile, the spectral signature astronomers use to spot any star blowing a wind.
card.wonder: It still looks this bright from over five thousand light-years away.
card.connect: WR 136, just over a degree away, has already blown off its outer layers.

lens.beat: On the brink: a star blowing itself apart
lens.question: How will P Cygni's struggle against its own light end?
lens.why: P Cygni is a heavyweight so luminous that it is already coming apart at the seams.
lens.answer: It will end with its core collapsing, after it has lost much more of itself. Its winds and outbursts strip away mass, like the shell of about a tenth of a Sun it threw off in 1600, and when the core has burned through its last fuel it will fall in on itself, most likely in a supernova.

stops.name: Dumbbell Nebula
stops.role: The end: what a star leaves behind

getThere.text: Move down and to the left about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (16°), and the Dumbbell Nebula is there, in Vulpecula.

stops.whyHere: The Dumbbell is what a star like the Sun leaves when it is done, close enough that binoculars show its shape on a dark, moonless night.
stops.transitionText: P Cygni has not yet crossed the edge, and the Dumbbell Nebula shows one of the two things a star can leave behind once it has.

card.question: Where is the easiest place to see how a Sun-like star dies?
card.glance: A small gray patch, clearly larger than any star, sometimes with a hint of a pinched apple-core shape.
card.see: Find the little arrow of Sagitta below Albireo, then move about 3° north of its tip star, γ Sagittae, into Vulpecula. The Dumbbell is a small, faint gray smudge; brace the binoculars and look slightly to one side, and on a dark night it turns squarish or hourglass-shaped.
card.understand: A star once like the Sun swelled into a giant and let its outer layers drift away, and its bare, extremely hot core now makes that gas glow like a neon sign. The outer shells are expanding at about 30 kilometers per second, and dividing the shell's size by that speed gives an age of roughly ten thousand years. Within tens of thousands more the gas will fade into space, carrying elements made inside the star.
card.answer: The Dumbbell may be the best place of all: a Sun-like star's shed layers, lit by its bare core and close enough, about 1,270 light-years, to show their shape in binoculars.
card.wonder: Its outer gas moves fast enough to cross the United States in under three minutes, yet from here the shape will look unchanged for your whole lifetime.
card.connect: Heavier stars go out violently; the Veil in Cygnus is the wreck of such an explosion.

lens.question: Is the Dumbbell the end of a star's story or a new beginning?
lens.why: The Dumbbell is what a star like the Sun leaves when it is done, close enough that binoculars show its shape on a dark, moonless night.
lens.answer: The Dumbbell is both. The white dwarf at its center will cool for billions of years and never shine by fusion again. But the gas, carrying elements made inside the star, will spread into the Galaxy's clouds, where future stars and planets will form from it, just as the Sun and Earth formed from material like this.
lens.story: The star at the Dumbbell's center is one of the hottest known, around a hundred thousand degrees, because it is the bare core that once burned helium deep inside the giant. Its ultraviolet light strips electrons from the gas around it, and as the core cools over the next tens of thousands of years the shell will dim until the glow goes out.

journeys.title: Splitting Cygnus Star by Star
journeys.drivingQuestion: When you see one star, how many are really there?
journeys.hook: Some pairs in the sky are partners in orbit, and some are strangers lined up by chance.
journeys.story: Your eye sees one point, binoculars see two, and patient measurement often finds more. The night runs from a first split toward a point of light that hides more suns than it shows, with the question of who belongs to whom along the way.
journeys.payoff: One star to the eye can be two in binoculars and several to physics, and a point that looks perfectly ordinary can hold a crowd of suns bound in orbits within orbits. The night's last stop made that concrete, a single point whose count runs past what any binoculars can show. The Sun, with no companion at all, turns out to be one of the quieter ways a star can live.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the west, around Cygnus

stops.name: Zeta Lyrae

getThere.text: Find Vega by eye, the brilliant blue-white star of Lyra, brightest of the Summer Triangle, about 45° up in the west. From there, hop up and to the left about 2° (a fraction of one field of your 6.5° binoculars) to Zeta Lyrae.

stops.whyHere: The first thing binoculars do is turn one star into two, and ζ Lyrae, a corner of Lyra's little parallelogram, is one of the friendliest places to watch it happen.

card.question: What makes a double star easy to split?
card.glance: A white star 2° south-east of Vega in Lyra that binoculars split into an unequal 44″ pair.
card.see: ζ Lyrae forms a small triangle with Vega and the Double-Double, at the top corner of Lyra's parallelogram. Binoculars show a brighter white star with a fainter companion just to the south-east.
card.understand: Two things decide a split: the gap and the difference in brightness. Here the gap is 44″, comfortably wide for binoculars though far tighter than the 3.5′ between the two halves of ε Lyrae next door. The companion is fainter but not overwhelmed, so it stands clear of the glare.
card.answer: A wide gap and a modest difference in brightness: ζ Lyrae's 44″ is easy for any binoculars, and its unequal pair makes the fainter star easy to pick out.
card.wonder: Its light left about 160 years ago, around the time the first telegraph cable across the Atlantic began carrying messages.
card.connect: Down the parallelogram lie red δ² Lyrae and variable Sheliak.

lens.question: Why does ζ Lyrae look single to the eye yet split in any binoculars?
lens.why: The first thing binoculars do is turn one star into two, and ζ Lyrae, a corner of Lyra's little parallelogram, is one of the friendliest places to watch it happen.
lens.look: ζ Lyrae makes a small triangle with Vega and the Double-Double. Binoculars split it into a white star with a fainter companion just to its south-east, clear at 10× and still separate at 7× if you hold steady.
lens.answer: That gap, around an eightieth of a degree, is one the unaided eye merges into a single point, while magnification spreads it into clear dark sky. The split gives you two white stars and nothing more; whether they are the same kind of star, or even near each other in space, takes a different kind of looking.

stops.name: 31 Cygni
stops.role: Two colors, two kinds of star

getThere.text: Sweep up about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (19°) to 31 Cygni, in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: 31 Cygni brings color into the counting, a group of stars wide enough for any binoculars in which one point glows orange and its neighbor shines white.
stops.transitionText: The split at Zeta Lyrae gave you two points; at 31 Cygni the two halves differ in color, and that difference is the first thing a split can measure.

card.question: Can binoculars show Albireo's colors with an easier split?
card.glance: An orange star 5° west-north-west of Deneb with a blue-white companion: a binocular color group with 30 Cygni.
card.see: Binoculars show orange 31 Cyg with white 30 Cyg about 5½′ away and a fainter star closer in. The gaps are wider than Albireo's, so the colors come easily.
card.understand: 31 Cygni is an orange supergiant, a cool star swollen to huge size. A hot blue star orbits it and slips behind it every 10.4 years. As the blue star sinks, its light shines for a while through the giant's thin outer atmosphere, so astronomers can probe that air like a lamp seen through fog.
card.answer: 31 Cygni does, pairing an orange supergiant with blue-white neighbors set wide enough for any binoculars.
card.wonder: The orange star is about 160 times wider than the Sun, so its true partner, a hot star far too close to split, takes weeks to slip behind it at each eclipse.
card.connect: Albireo shows the same colors at a tighter split.

lens.question: Why does 31 Cygni glow orange beside its white neighbor 30 Cygni?
lens.why: 31 Cygni brings color into the counting, a group of stars wide enough for any binoculars in which one point glows orange and its neighbor shines white.
lens.look: About five degrees west-north-west of Deneb, binoculars show orange 31 Cygni with white 30 Cygni about five and a half minutes of arc away and a fainter star closer in, under two minutes from the orange one. The gaps are wide, so the colors come easily even at 7×.
lens.answer: Orange means a cool surface and white a much hotter one, so the two points are different kinds of star before you know anything else about them. Whether the white neighbor and the fainter star belong to the orange one is not known, because color tells you what a star is, never whose company it keeps.
lens.story: Starlight is a broad rainbow, not a single color, and a star's temperature only shifts where the peak of that rainbow falls. A cool star like 31 Cygni peaks near the red end, so it looks orange, while a much hotter star such as its white neighbor spreads its light across the colors evenly enough that the eye blends them into white. That is also why no star ever looks green: a star whose light peaks in the green still shines strongly in red and blue, and the mixture reads as white.

stops.name: 16 Cygni

getThere.text: From 31 Cygni, slide down and to the right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°) to 16 Cygni, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: 16 Cygni is a pair of Sun-like stars that shows partnership at its most convincing, because the evidence tying the two together comes from three separate directions.
stops.transitionText: Two colors at 31 Cygni meant two kinds of star, and at 16 Cygni the pair shows what it takes to call two stars partners.

card.question: What would our Sun be like with a twin beside it?
card.glance: One of a matched pair of 6th-magnitude yellowish stars 40″ apart, on the swan's western wing in Cygnus.
card.see: From δ Cygni, go about 5° north with the chart to a pair of equal faint stars 40″ apart, split at 10× on a steady mount. Both share a soft yellow-white tint, and 16 Cyg B is the slightly fainter one, to the south-east.
card.understand: Both stars are close copies of the Sun in temperature and mass. Stars ring like bells, and since the tones depend on what is inside, the Kepler spacecraft's measurements of their tiny pulsations gave both an age of about 6.8 billion years, older than the Sun. In 1996 astronomers found a planet at least 1.5 times Jupiter's mass circling B once every 2.2 years on a strongly stretched orbit.

card.question: How many stars can hide inside one faint point of light?
card.glance: Two matching white stars about 1.7° north-east of Vega in Lyra; any binoculars split them.

journeys.title: The Colors of Hydrus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Can you read a star's temperature just by looking at its color?
journeys.hook: In the sky red means cool and blue means hot, the reverse of every bathroom tap.
journeys.story: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then yellow, then white, and the hottest stars go further still, to blue-white. Tonight you climb the scale from the warm glow of Tiaki, judging each tint first and learning its temperature after, until the eye's thermometer reaches the top of its range.
journeys.payoff: Stars differ in color because their surfaces differ in temperature, and tonight the scale ran from Tiaki all the way to Achernar at the hot end. There, every square meter of a star's surface outshines the Sun's many times over. Near the top the tints crowded together even as the temperatures leapt, which is the eye reaching the limit of its range. Astronomers carry on from there with spectra, but the first reading of every star is still the one you took tonight, its color.

stops.name: Tiaki

getThere.text: Find Tiaki by eye, the red star of Grus, the Crane, about 45° up in the south-west. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: In Grus the whole thermometer fits in two quick glances, and the reading starts here, with the Crane's ember-colored star.

card.question: Why is the red star of the Crane cooler than the white one beside it?
card.glance: The orange-red star of Grus, the Crane, six degrees from blue-white Alnair, a ready-made color contrast.
card.see: Put Tiaki and Alnair in turn at the center of your binoculars: Tiaki is a deep orange-red, Alnair a clean blue-white. Defocus slightly and the colors strengthen, and over weeks you can watch Tiaki’s brightness wander a little.
card.understand: Tiaki is a red giant near the end of its life, swollen to about 150 times the Sun’s width. Its surface is only about 3,500 K, so it glows orange-red. Blacksmiths know the rule: iron glows red first and white only when far hotter, and stars follow the same physics.
card.answer: In stars, color is a thermometer that runs opposite to the bathroom tap, so red Tiaki is the cool one, far cooler than blue-white Alnair beside it.
card.wonder: Its swollen outer layers heave on a rough rhythm of about 37 days, nudging its brightness up and down.
card.connect: Its puffed-up outer layers are already drifting away, and L² Puppis shows a star further down the same road.

lens.question: How much cooler is the Crane's red star than its blue-white neighbor?
lens.why: In Grus the whole thermometer fits in two quick glances, and the reading starts here, with the Crane's ember-colored star.
lens.look: Put Tiaki and Alnair in turn at the center of your binoculars. Tiaki is a deep orange-red, Alnair a clean blue-white, and a slight defocus makes both colors richer.
lens.answer: Alnair runs at about 13,200 K, nearly four times Tiaki's temperature, and your eye turns that difference into the contrast between ember and ice.
lens.story: Every glowing body has a color at which its light peaks, and the peak slides toward shorter waves as the temperature climbs. lens.question: Why is Alpha Tucanae orange, and how hot does that make it?
lens.why: In the quiet far south near the Small Magellanic Cloud, an orange giant stands alone and gives the scale its next mark.
lens.look: Alpha Tucanae is a soft orange point standing alone in Tucana. Defocus slightly, then sweep about 13° north to blue-white Alnair in Grus and back, and the warm tint holds.
lens.answer: Alpha Tucanae's surface runs some 1,600 degrees cooler than the Sun's, the skin of a giant that cooled as it swelled, so its glow tilts toward orange. Alnair, to the north, is about three times hotter.
lens.story: A lone star's color is hard to judge, because the eye has nothing to compare it with, and that is why observers sweep from Alpha Tucanae to a hotter neighbor and back. stops.name: Beta Hydri

card.question: What will the Sun be like a few billion years from now?
card.glance: A modest yellowish star in Hydrus near the south celestial pole, close to the Small Magellanic Cloud.
card.see: Beta Hydri sits near the south celestial pole, roughly between the Small Magellanic Cloud and the pole. Binoculars show a soft yellow star, the tint the Sun would show at night, and about 5° away lies the Small Cloud’s misty glow.
card.understand: Beta Hydri rings gently like a bell, its surface rising and falling in tiny oscillations that the TESS satellite detected in its light. The pitch of those tones depends on the star’s size and density, so they weigh and date it: about 1.1 Suns of mass and about 6.5 billion years old. It has finished burning hydrogen in its core and is slowly swelling, already almost twice the Sun’s width.
card.answer: Much like Beta Hydri, an older Sun already over three times as bright as ours, a stage our own star will reach in a few billion years.
card.wonder: It also has a 12-year cycle of magnetic activity, much like the Sun’s own.
card.connect: Further down the Sun’s road lie bigger, shedding giants such as L² Puppis.

lens.question: Is Beta Hydri's soft yellow the same color as our Sun?
lens.why: Near the south celestial pole shines a Sun-like star whose color you can treat as the Sun's own at night.
lens.look: Beta Hydri sits near the south celestial pole, roughly between the Small Magellanic Cloud and the pole. Binoculars show a soft yellow star, the tint the Sun would show at night, with the Small Cloud's misty glow about 5° away.
lens.answer: Its surface is about 5,800 K, matching the Sun's to within a few dozen degrees, so this soft yellow is the Sun's own color seen at night. Anything whiter is hotter than our star, anything more orange cooler.

card.question: What happens to a star that spins almost fast enough to fly apart?
card.glance: An icy blue-white star shining alone, low in the far south.
card.see: Look for the lone brilliant blue-white star at the end of the long, faint river of Eridanus. Binoculars show only a sharp point, so enjoy its icy color and compare it with creamy Alpha Hydri about 5° away.
card.understand: Achernar is a hot star about six times the Sun’s mass, spinning near the speed at which it would fling itself apart. As with a spinning pizza dough, the spin pushes its equator outward into a bulge. Interferometers at the VLT combined telescopes to measure its outline and found it longer one way than the other, the flattest star resolved at the time.
card.answer: It flattens and leaks, Achernar’s equator bulging about a third wider than its poles and, from time to time, shedding a thin disk of gas from that waist. Pushed far enough, a star starts to come apart at the seams.
card.wonder: It is only about 63 million years old, while the Sun has already lived some 70 times longer.
card.connect: A smaller companion swings around it every seven years, and its orbit is how astronomers weighed Achernar.

resolved.story: Achernar spins so fast that it is flattened, and a flattened star is hotter at its poles than at its stretched-out waist, by many thousands of degrees in its case. The blue-white you see is an average over that patchwork, weighted by how the star happens to be tilted toward us.
resolved.understand: Achernar is a hot star about six times the Sun’s mass, spinning near the speed at which it would fling itself apart. As with a spinning pizza dough, the spin pushes its equator outward into a bulge. Interferometers at the VLT combined telescopes to measure its outline and found it longer one way than the other, the flattest star resolved at the time.
resolved.answer: Achernar's surface is about 14,800 K, roughly two and a half times the Sun's temperature, so its glow tips firmly toward blue, the hot end of the scale in this part of the sky.
resolved.wonder: It is only about 63 million years old, while the Sun has already lived some 70 times longer.
resolved.payoff: Stars differ in color because their surfaces differ in temperature, and tonight the scale ran from Tiaki all the way to Achernar at the hot end. Astronomers carry on from there with spectra, but the first reading of every star is still the one you took tonight, its color.

journeys.title: The Star Families of Orion
journeys.drivingQuestion: Do star families stay together, or do they drift apart?
journeys.hook: Every star cluster is a family photograph, and the older the photo, the fewer remain.
journeys.story: Stars are born in families, but they do not stay in them. Starting at σ Orionis, tonight follows families still held together by their own gravity out to siblings so widely scattered that only the way they move shows they are kin.
journeys.payoff: From σ Orionis to Orion’s Belt, the night ended where every family of stars ends, scattered across the sky and tied together only by the way its members move. Astronomers can still find such siblings because a shared birth leaves two lasting marks, a common motion that fades only slowly and a common chemistry that never fades at all. The Sun's family dispersed so long ago that its motion has been forgotten, so the search for its siblings now rests on chemistry alone.

stops.name: σ Orionis

getThere.text: Find Orion’s Belt by eye, the row of three bright stars across the middle of Orion, about 35° up in the north-east. From there, hop up about 2° (a fraction of one field of your 6.5° binoculars) to σ Orionis.

stops.whyHere: σ Orionis sits at the center of one of Orion's youngest families, about three million years old, and it shows how tightly some newborn siblings stay bound.

card.question: How many stars hide in the single point of σ Orionis?
card.glance: A small knot of stars just south-west of Alnitak, the left-hand Belt star.
card.see: From Alnitak, drop about 1° south-west to a small knot of stars. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east; a closer one due east, and many more, need a telescope.
card.understand: The central pair is far too close for any ordinary telescope, but interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, have traced its orbit. Combine the size of that orbit on the sky with spectra that clock the stars’ speeds, and you get masses of about 17 and 13 Suns. The distance comes as a bonus, because the orbit’s true size in kilometers and its apparent size in arcseconds can only match at one distance.
card.answer: At least five stars are bound together here, and the central pair’s orbit pins the young cluster’s distance at about 1,260 light-years with rare precision.
card.wonder: Around the bright star swarm dozens of faint brown dwarfs, failed stars too small to burn hydrogen, born from the same cloud.
card.connect: The same young family stretches along the Belt just above.

lens.beat: Born together: a household within a family
lens.question: Is the bright star σ Orionis one sibling, or a whole household of them?
lens.why: σ Orionis sits at the center of one of Orion's youngest families, about three million years old, and it shows how tightly some newborn siblings stay bound.
lens.look: From Alnitak drop about a degree south-west to a small knot of stars. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east, and the scatter of faint stars around it is the rest of its family.
lens.answer: It is a whole household. At least five stars are bound together in that one point, the heaviest siblings still locked in orbit while the cluster's lighter members spread around them, and the tighter such a bond, the longer it survives what time does to the rest of the family.
lens.story: Telling σ Orionis's siblings from the stars in front of and behind it relies on the marks of youth. Very young stars of modest mass still hold the lithium they were born with, flare brightly in X-rays and are often still wrapped in dusty disks that glow in the infrared, so a faint star near σ Orionis that shows all three is almost certainly kin. Counted this way the family runs to a few hundred members, most of them far too faint for binoculars.

stops.name: NGC 1981

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: NGC 1981 is already in the same view, just above σ Orionis.

stops.whyHere: NGC 1981 sits just north of the Orion Nebula, where siblings are still being born, so it shows the very next stage: a young family standing in clear space.
stops.transitionText: NGC 1981 is another family born in a single burst, like σ Orionis, and two litters seen one after the other make it plain that this is simply how stars arrive.

card.question: What happens to a star family after its birth cloud is gone?
card.glance: A loose handful of stars at the top of Orion’s Sword, with no glow around them.
card.see: Move about a degree north of the Orion Nebula, to the top of Orion’s Sword. A sparse group of a dozen stars stands there, clean and haze-free on a dark background.
card.understand: NGC 1981 is an open cluster, a loose family of stars born together about four and a half million years ago. Gaia’s parallaxes put it just in front of the Orion Nebula. Within a few million years of birth, a young group’s hottest stars blow the leftover gas away like a gust clearing fog from a valley.
card.answer: It stands in the open: NGC 1981 is a bare handful of siblings whose hottest stars blew their leftover gas away.
card.wonder: In a few million years the Orion Nebula’s own stars should look like this.
card.connect: Even bigger siblings of this family shine in Orion’s Belt.

lens.beat: Born together: fresh out of the cloud
lens.question: What does a star family look like once its birth cloud has just gone?
lens.why: NGC 1981 sits just north of the Orion Nebula, where siblings are still being born, so it shows the very next stage: a young family standing in clear space.
lens.look: Center the top of Orion's Sword, a degree north of the nebula. A sparse group of about a dozen stars stands clean against a dark background, with none of the glow that wraps the nebula just south.
lens.answer: It looks bare and a little ragged: a few million years have been enough for its hottest stars to blow the gas away. It is one of several waves of star birth in Orion's great family, each wave a litter of its own.
lens.story: Orion's great family was born in a sequence. Its subgroups grow younger from the north-west toward the Sword, as if star birth had been sweeping through the cloud, perhaps set off each time by the light and blasts of the generation before. This little group belongs to one of the younger waves, near the front of that sweep, with the youngest of all still forming in the nebula just south.

stops.name: Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster

getThere.text: Move left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (19°), and the Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster is there, still in Orion.

stops.whyHere: The Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster is an old family at the same distance as Orion's young ones, so the difference you see beside the Sword is age alone. This is the night's challenge, and if it will not show after a patient minute, move on.
stops.transitionText: NGC 1981 is a family still close together; at the Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster the question becomes how well a family stands up to the steady pull of the Milky Way.

card.question: What does a star family look like a few hundred million years on?
card.glance: A small, sparse group of stars on the western edge of Orion.
card.see: Start at π² Orionis in Orion’s shield, the arc of faint stars west of Bellatrix, and move about two degrees north. A small group of faint stars stands out; the spaceship outline needs more magnification.
card.understand: This family is a few hundred million years old, and its hottest, heaviest stars, which live fastest, have already died. Gaia counts a few hundred members, all drifting together. At about 1,320 light-years it lies almost exactly as far away as the Orion Nebula, so the difference you see is age alone.
card.answer: It looks sparse and quiet, its blazing stars gone and its fainter siblings slowly spreading out.
card.wonder: When these stars were born, the first four-legged animals had only lately hauled themselves out of the water, and no backboned animal had yet laid an egg on dry land.
card.connect: The Belt’s young blue giants, nearby, show the same kind of family in its youth.

lens.question: What will Orion's bright young families look like a few hundred million years from now?
lens.why: The Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster is an old family at the same distance as Orion's young ones, so the difference you see beside the Sword is age alone.
lens.look: From π² Orionis, in the arc of faint stars west of Bellatrix, move about two degrees north to a small group of faint stars. Nothing in it is blue and brilliant; compare it in your mind with the Sword's bright young stars.
lens.answer: They will look much like this: a sparse little group whose heaviest stars died long ago, its fainter siblings slowly spreading into the Milky Way. The Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster has already lived through that stretch of time, and it shows that the bright families of Orion's Sword are a passing stage.
lens.story: Only a small part of Orion's present families is likely to end up like this one. Most of the young stars around the Sword and the Belt were born in loose groups that are already unbound and spreading, and only the densest knots, such as the cluster at the heart of the Orion Nebula, may hold enough mass to stay together for hundreds of millions of years. A family like this is what the lucky survivors of such a region look like.

stops.name: Hyades

getThere.text: Move left about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (7°), and the Hyades is there, in Taurus.

stops.whyHere: The Hyades are the nearest star family of all, and an old one, so this is where you can watch a family thinning out with your own eyes.
stops.transitionText: The Hyades has spent longer under the galaxy's pull than the Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster, so the two together show how that contest goes as the years pile up.

card.question: How can a cluster’s colors tell its age?
card.glance: A big V of stars spilling past the edges of the field, several of them yellow-orange.
card.see: The V of the Bull’s face in Taurus is too big for one view, so sweep along each arm. A few cluster stars are tinted orange among the white ones. Aldebaran, the brightest orange point at one tip, is the odd one out.
card.understand: Because the Hyades are so close, the Hipparcos satellite could measure the parallax of individual members and map the cluster in three dimensions, with its core about 150 light-years away. The family is about 625 million years old, five times older than the Pleiades. In that time its heaviest blue stars have died, and the next heaviest have swollen into orange giants.
card.answer: The color of the brightest members is the clock: blue-white stars mean the heavy ones are still alive, while orange giants among white and yellow stars mean that era has passed.
card.wonder: Gaia has traced stars escaping from it into two long tails, one leading and one trailing the cluster along its orbit, each stretching for hundreds of light-years.
card.connect: The brightest star in the V, Aldebaran, does not belong to the family at all.

lens.question: How much of the Hyades family is still held together by its own gravity?
lens.why: The Hyades are the nearest star family of all, and an old one, so this is where you can watch a family thinning out with your own eyes.
lens.look: Sweep along the two arms of the Bull's V-shaped face; the family is too big for one field. Among its white and yellowish members a few are tinted orange, its aged giants, while bright orange Aldebaran at one tip is an outsider standing in front.
lens.answer: Gravity still holds only part of the family. Gaia counts nearly a thousand members, yet only about 190 Suns' worth of stars is still within the cluster's gravitational grip, and the rest are working their way out into the Milky Way. At about 625 million years, the Hyades are a family in their last chapters as a cluster.
lens.story: The Hyades are near enough for every member to be placed in three dimensions, so astronomers can draw the boundary where the family's own gravity gives way to the galaxy's tide, about 26 light-years from the center, and simply count who lies inside it. A large share of the family already lies outside, on its way out, and the members still gathered near the middle are mostly the heavier ones, because in a family that has lived this long the lightest siblings are always the first to be pushed to the edge and lost.
