stops.name: Orion’s Belt
stops.plainClass: loose family of young, hot stars

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about three and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (24°) to Orion’s Belt, in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Orion's Belt marks the heart of a young family of a different kind from a cluster: hot, heavy siblings spread across several degrees of sky, the brightest family of the winter sky.
stops.transitionText: Where the Hyades still holds its family together, at least in part, Orion’s Belt belongs to one whose members are scattered across the sky and tied together only by the way they move.

card.question: Are the three stars of Orion’s Belt really a family?
card.glance: Three bright blue-white stars in a row, sprinkled with dozens of fainter ones.
card.see: Put the middle Belt star in the center and let the outer two sit near the edges. An S-shaped chain of fainter stars winds through the field, and many of them belong to the same young group.
card.understand: The Belt stars are among the heaviest stars you can see: young, very hot and burning their fuel quickly. They belong to an OB association, a loose spread of young star groups across Orion born in several waves, the Belt’s wave about five million years ago. Gaia has since untangled the field into several groups moving together at slightly different distances, so the family turns out to have branches.
card.answer: They are a family, though a loose one: young, heavy siblings from the same cloud complex as the Orion Nebula, which gravity does not hold together, so they are slowly drifting apart.
card.wonder: These stars will be gone within a few million years, while the Sun still has billions ahead of it.
card.connect: Heavy stars live fast, and Betelgeuse, up on Orion’s shoulder, shows one near the end.

lens.question: Will the Belt stars and their young siblings stay together as they age?
lens.why: Orion's Belt marks the heart of a young family of a different kind from a cluster: hot, heavy siblings spread across several degrees of sky, the brightest family of the winter sky.
lens.look: Put the middle Belt star at the center and let the outer two sit near the edges. An S-shaped chain of fainter stars winds through the field, and many of them share the Belt stars' blue-white color and their birth.
lens.answer: These siblings will not stay together. An association like this is born too loose for its own gravity to hold, so they are already drifting apart while only a few million years old, and in time they will spread across whole constellations, tied together only by the direction they travel.
lens.story: That a group like this is flying apart was shown by its motions. In the 1950s Adriaan Blaauw found that the stars of such associations move outward from a common center, like fragments of a slow explosion, and running the motions backward gave the time since they were together, a second clock alongside the ages read from the stars themselves. Gaia has since measured those motions for thousands of members across Orion and found the same pattern, branch by branch.

journeys.title: Finding Our Place in the Galaxy from Cassiopeia
journeys.drivingQuestion: How can you tell where we live in a galaxy you can never leave?
journeys.hook: The Milky Way's band is our own galaxy's disk, seen edge-on from the inside.
journeys.story: Every star you can see without a telescope belongs to the Milky Way, and tonight's path leaves it behind at the very end, for another galaxy seen across intergalactic space. Everything before that last view is a survey of our own galaxy, carried out from the inside.
journeys.payoff: The Milky Way is a barred spiral, and we live in its thin disk, in a modest arm about halfway out, with a halo of ancient swarms around everything. Nobody can step outside to check, so astronomers built that picture from inside and then compared it with other galaxies, seen whole across intergalactic space. Tonight you did the same, ending on a galaxy beyond our own, which means you have looked at our home from both sides of its edge.

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Find the Alpha Persei Cluster by eye, the spray of stars around Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, about 65° up in the north-east. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The Alpha Persei Cluster is one of the nearest young star families to the Sun, and it is still rich in the kind of stars that cannot be old.

card.question: What does a star family look like from up close?
card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains. It is too big for most telescopes to frame, so binoculars or the eye alone take it in whole.
card.understand: This is an open cluster, a family of stars born together from one cloud, and Gaia picks out its members by their shared motion, like spotting a family walking together through a crowd. Its age comes from a subtle clue: the lightest members slowly destroy the lithium inside them, so the line between stars that still have lithium and those that have lost it works like a clock. Here it reads about 90 million years.
card.answer: Like the Alpha Persei Cluster: at 566 light-years its members spread over several Moon widths, a spray only binoculars can frame. Farther away, the same family would shrink into a small knot.
card.wonder: This family was born while dinosaurs still had tens of millions of years left.
card.connect: The Double Cluster, more than ten times farther away, shows how small a star family looks from across the galaxy.

lens.question: Is the Sun's neighborhood still turning out young star families?
lens.why: The Alpha Persei Cluster is one of the nearest young star families to the Sun, and it is still rich in the kind of stars that cannot be old.
lens.look: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too wide for most telescopes but just right for binoculars. Blue-white stars burn out fast, so a crowd of them is a young crowd.
lens.answer: Our neighborhood made this family only recently: the Alpha Persei Cluster, about 566 light-years away, still holds hot blue-white members that burn through their fuel quickly, so stars were being born in our part of the disk not long ago by a galaxy's standards. stops.name: Stock 2

getThere.text: Move up and to the left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°), and Stock 2 is there, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Stock 2 is a big, loose family just north of the Double Cluster, and the pair is the clearest demonstration in the northern sky of how deep the band runs.
stops.transitionText: Leave the neighbors around the Alpha Persei Cluster behind and look farther out, to Stock 2, in the Sun's own stretch of the disk.

card.question: Are two clusters side by side in the sky really neighbors?
card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars in Cassiopeia, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north, and a large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the “Muscleman”. Use the widest field you have, because a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Gaia measures each member’s parallax and averages them, which pins down a cluster’s distance far better than any single star could. For Stock 2 it gives about 1,200 light-years, and for the Double Cluster over 7,000. The ages differ too: Stock 2 has lost its hottest blue stars, a sign of a few hundred million years, while the Double Cluster’s still blaze.
card.answer: These two are not: Stock 2 is about six times nearer and far older than the glittering pair beside it, proof that clusters touching on the sky can live in completely different parts of the galaxy.
card.wonder: Gaia found about 3,000 members here, a big family hiding in plain sight because it is so spread out.
card.connect: Swing back to the Double Cluster: the nearer family looks bigger and looser, the farther one smaller and denser.

lens.question: Stock 2 and the Double Cluster share a sweep, but do they share an arm?

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

stops.whyHere: The Owl Cluster's bright eye, φ Cassiopeiae, shows to the naked eye on a dark night, and whether it belongs to the cluster decides how far away that eye is.

card.question: Does the Owl Cluster’s bright eye really belong to the cluster?
card.glance: Two bright “eyes” at one end of a small, elongated swarm in Cassiopeia, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other; the bright one is φ Cassiopeiae. A faint, slightly elongated spray trails away from them, and steady binoculars turn it into outstretched wings or arms.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,100 light-years away and only about 23 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life; if it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia’s parallax for φ Cas matches the cluster’s, but very bright stars are hard for Gaia to measure, and its speed toward us differs somewhat from older values.
card.answer: Probably, since the evidence leans toward membership, which would make the owl’s eye one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. The case is not closed, and that is part of the fun.
card.wonder: If φ Cas is a member, its light set out about 9,100 years ago, when one of the first towns, Çatalhöyük in Anatolia, was taking shape.
card.connect: M103, a degree from Ruchbah, is a cluster whose stars clearly belong together.

lens.beat: The next arm out, to the naked eye
lens.question: Can you see a single star in another spiral arm with your own eyes?
lens.why: The Owl Cluster's bright eye, φ Cassiopeiae, shows to the naked eye on a dark night, and whether it belongs to the cluster decides how far away that eye is.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: From the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), slide up and to the left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (18°) to the Andromeda Galaxy, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest big spiral to ours, and it is the one place in the sky where you can take in the whole shape of a galaxy like our own.
stops.transitionText: The Owl Cluster still lies in our galaxy's disk, while the Andromeda Galaxy is a galaxy of its own, far beyond every star of ours.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

lens.question: What would the Milky Way look like from far outside?
lens.why: The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest big spiral to ours, and it is the one place in the sky where you can take in the whole shape of a galaxy like our own.
lens.look: From Mirach, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears: an oval core with a haze stretching about three degrees under averted vision. That haze is a tilted disk of stars, the same kind of disk we live inside.
lens.answer: From far outside, the Milky Way would look much like Andromeda: a flattened spiral disk around a bright central bulge, wrapped in a faint halo. From Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away, our own galaxy would be a similar smudge with the Sun lost about halfway out in its disk, and every clue you can gather from inside, the disk, the arms, the halo, is laid out here in one glance.
lens.story: Andromeda lets astronomers check from outside what they infer from inside: its dust lanes, the young clusters along its arms and its old central bulge show up plainly in photographs. Its halo of globular clusters is there too, a few hundred of them, two to three times as many as ours.

journeys.title: Look-Alikes of Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: When two lights in the sky look alike, how can you tell them apart?
journeys.hook: Two lights can look like twins and be strangers; tonight you learn to tell them apart.
journeys.story: A nearby modest star and a distant giant can look like a matched pair, because the sky hides how deep it is. Tonight you take such pairs apart one clue at a time, and the same clues end the night by unmasking a soft glow, which turns out to be something quite unlike its neighbors.
journeys.payoff: Brightness alone could not be trusted, because it mixes a star's true power with its distance, while color, short of a little reddening by dust, held up as an honest thermometer of a star's surface. At the Andromeda Galaxy the same suspicion sorted out a glow, whose brightness gave little away until its texture, size and setting revealed what kind of thing it is. The flat sky is a deep one, full of strangers standing shoulder to shoulder, and next time two lights look like a matched pair you will know to ask how far away each one is.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Cepheus

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: Find Alderamin by eye, the brightest star of Cepheus, about 50° up in the north-west. From there, hop right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (8°) to Alfirk.

stops.whyHere: Alfirk sits partway up the house of Cepheus from Alderamin, its bright corner, and beside that neighbor it looks like the lesser star, the kind of judgment the eye makes without thinking.

card.question: Can a star pulse every few hours without anyone noticing?
card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: β Cephei lies in Cepheus between Alderamin and Errai, and binoculars show a blue-white point. Its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, needs a small telescope.
card.understand: Deep in β Cep’s layers, iron atoms trap heat when squeezed and release it when they expand, and that valve keeps the star ringing like a bell. The ringing shows up as a rhythm in its light and in the speed of its surface. Its light changes by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.
card.answer: It can, and for most of history nobody noticed, since β Cephei rings every 4.57 hours too faintly for any eye.
card.wonder: Alfirk rings like a bell several times a day, and astronomers read that ringing the way seismologists read earthquakes, to probe the hidden inside of a hot star.
card.connect: δ Cephei, in the same constellation, pulses slowly and deeply enough to follow by eye.

lens.question: Is Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, also its most powerful?
lens.why: Alfirk sits partway up the house of Cepheus from Alderamin, its bright corner, and beside that neighbor it looks like the lesser star, the kind of judgment the eye makes without thinking.
lens.look: Put Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, in the field and then move to Alfirk, nearly a magnitude fainter and a little bluer. Both look like ordinary points, and nothing in their light says how far each has traveled.
lens.answer: Alderamin only looks the stronger because it is near: Alfirk lies about fourteen times farther away, near 685 light-years against 49, and gives out about a thousand times more light, roughly 19,000 Suns against 18. The brighter-looking star is simply the closer one, a trap the eye falls into again and again.
lens.story: A hot star hides much of its power from the eye, because most of its light comes out as ultraviolet, beyond violet, where we see nothing at all, so Alfirk's visible glow is only a fraction of its true output. Here the brightness clue misleads twice, once through distance and once through the colors the eye cannot see.

stops.name: δ Cephei
stops.plainClass: yellow supergiant + blue-white star, pulsating Cepheid

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°) to δ Cephei, still in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: δ Cephei carries its own color comparison, a fainter blue-white companion close beside it, so in one steady view you can read two temperatures from a pair of stars that travel together.
stops.transitionText: Distance fooled the eye at Alfirk, so at δ Cephei the test turns to color, which reaches you unchanged however far the light has come.

card.question: How did a star that pulses every five days become a ruler for the universe?
card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a blue-white companion beside it, brightening and fading on a strict five-day rhythm.
card.see: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house-shaped figure of Cepheus, with a fainter blue-white companion close beside it. Over several nights compare it with ζ Cephei, its match at peak, and ε Cephei, its match at the bottom, and you will see it brighten quickly and fade slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen late in life, and its outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt studied many such stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, all at nearly the same distance, so any difference in how bright they looked had to be real. The slower a star beat, she found, the brighter it truly was: time the pulse and you know its real power.
card.answer: Know a lamp’s true wattage, and how faint it looks tells you how far away it is. When Edwin Hubble caught the same beat in a star inside the Andromeda “nebula”, the universe grew enormously overnight.
card.wonder: Its cousins in distant galaxies still anchor the measurement of how fast the universe is expanding.
card.connect: β Cephei, elsewhere in the same constellation, pulses too, but every few hours and so gently that only instruments can tell.

lens.question: Why is δ Cephei yellowish while the small companion beside it is blue-white?
lens.why: δ Cephei carries its own color comparison, a fainter blue-white companion close beside it, so in one steady view you can read two temperatures from a pair of stars that travel together.
lens.look: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house of Cepheus. Brace your binoculars and look for the fainter companion close beside the yellowish star; at 10× the pair splits, and the contrast between yellow and blue-white is the thing to judge.
lens.answer: The bright star's surface is about 5,820 K, close to the Sun's, so it glows yellowish, while its companion is a hotter star whose light leans blue. The two share a motion through space, so their colors differ because of what they are, not where they are.
lens.story: δ Cephei's own color drifts as it pulses, warmer when it is dim and whiter when it is bright, a change precise light meters record though the eye cannot. Color and brightness move together because both come from the surface heating and cooling, and that link helped show the star is really breathing rather than being eclipsed by its companion.

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (11°), and ρ Cassiopeiae is there, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint star near Caph, and η Cassiopeiae in the W have surfaces of about the same temperature, which makes the pair a clean test of size once you see past a tint that dust has warmed.
stops.transitionText: Color gave you a temperature at δ Cephei, and at ρ Cassiopeiae you put it together with true brightness, and out comes a star's size.

card.question: How can a star you can barely see be one of the sky’s most powerful?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia that looks entirely ordinary.
card.see: Start at Caph, the western end of Cassiopeia’s W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to a faint yellowish star. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of Caroline’s Rose between them.
card.understand: Most stars that look bright are simply close, and ρ Cas is the opposite case. Astronomers fix its distance from the family of stars it travels with and measure its true width with interferometers, and together those give its real output. A star this extreme, roughly 40 times the Sun’s mass, lives in a brief, unstable late stage, and in 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.
card.answer: From about 9,000 light-years away, a star needs more than half a million times the Sun’s output to reach your eye at all, and ρ Cassiopeiae has it. The faint dot near Caph is one of the most luminous stars you can see.
card.wonder: That single outburst in 2000 shed gas weighing roughly 10,000 Earths.
card.connect: Power, not closeness, puts it in your sky: η Cassiopeiae, brighter to the eye, is only about 19 light-years away.

lens.beat: The Sun's heat, a giant's size
lens.question: ρ and η Cassiopeiae are about equally hot; why is one so much stronger?
lens.why: ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint star near Caph, and η Cassiopeiae in the W have surfaces of about the same temperature, which makes the pair a clean test of size once you see past a tint that dust has warmed.
lens.look: Start at Caph and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint yellow-orange point. Then swing back east to η Cassiopeiae, between Schedar and γ in the W, a brighter, paler yellow star. ρ looks the warmer of the two, partly because dust along its long path reddens it.
lens.answer: At the same temperature a star's light grows with its surface, and ρ Cassiopeiae gives out hundreds of thousands of times as much as η: it is about 630 times the Sun's width, against η's slightly more than one. resolved.question: ρ and η Cassiopeiae are about equally hot; why is one so much stronger?
resolved.transition: Color gave you a temperature at δ Cephei, and at ρ Cassiopeiae you put it together with true brightness, and out comes a star's size.
resolved.why: ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint star near Caph, and η Cassiopeiae in the W have surfaces of about the same temperature, which makes the pair a clean test of size once you see past a tint that dust has warmed.
resolved.look: Start at Caph and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to ρ Cassiopeiae, a faint yellow-orange point. card.question: Why do a few orange stars shine among the Double Cluster’s blue-white crowd?
card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view between Cassiopeia and Perseus, a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia’s W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points, the western one, h Persei, a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so all their stars share a birthday. Most are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun, and the orange points are the heaviest of all. Weight is destiny for a star: the more massive it is, the faster it burns, so those few have already raced to their last chapter.
card.answer: The orange stars were born with the rest, but being the heaviest they aged fastest and have swollen into red supergiants, cool on the surface and orange in color. Their ages, read from the supergiants alone, match the cluster’s, a neat cross-check.
card.wonder: They lie about 7,400 light-years away, more than ten times farther than the Pleiades, yet are still bright enough to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Its twin, χ Persei, sits half a degree east, born of the same cloud at the same time.

lens.question: In a family only 14 million years old, how can some stars already be dying giants?
lens.why: The Double Cluster packs hundreds of stars with one birthday into a single binocular field, so the few that look different are telling you something about weight, not age.
lens.look: Sweep from Cassiopeia's W toward Perseus and hold both clusters in one field. Among the blue-white crowd look for a few orange stars, especially toward the eastern cluster, and defocus a touch to make their color plain.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Move up and to the left about three and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (22°), and the Andromeda Galaxy is there, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: In binoculars the Andromeda Galaxy is a gray oval surrounded by ordinary stars, and nothing in the view says that the glow and the stars belong to entirely different worlds.
stops.transitionText: After the star families of the Double Cluster, the Andromeda Galaxy is a glow that only looks like one of them, and every clue so far is needed to unmask it.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

lens.question: Andromeda's glow and the stars around it share a field; how far apart are they?
lens.why: In binoculars the Andromeda Galaxy is a gray oval surrounded by ordinary stars, and nothing in the view says that the glow and the stars belong to entirely different worlds.
lens.look: From Mirach climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears: a bright oval core with haze stretching to either side. Compare it with the sharp stars sprinkled across the field, and look for M32, a fuzzy star just south of the core.
lens.answer: Mirach, the star that leads you to the glow, lies about 200 light-years away, while the Andromeda Galaxy's light set out about 2.5 million years ago, more than ten thousand times farther. M32, the fuzzy star beside it, is a small galaxy in its own right, so one binocular field mixes our galaxy's stars with another galaxy and its companion.

resolved.payoff: Brightness alone could not be trusted, because it mixes a star's true power with its distance, while color, short of a little reddening by dust, held up as an honest thermometer of a star's surface.
